20   Q.   Please explain the importance of the allowable return on equity and its relationship
21        to the cost of equity.
22   A.   The “cost of capital” for a firm is an estimate of the cost of obtaining the capital required

                                                                          Direct Testimony of Tyler Comings


 1           to fund that firm’s operations and maintain financial strength. Firms that require

 2           substantial, upfront capital acquire it through the issuance of debt (in the form of bonds) or

 3           equity (in the form of shares). Bondholders and shareholders provide an infusion of capital

 4           to the firm, but they require returns on their bonds and shares that are commensurate with

 5           the underlying risks of those investments, respectively. The firm’s “cost of capital” is the

 6           fair and reasonable level of return at which investors would provide sufficient capital—

 7           thus it is composed of the “cost of debt” and the “cost of equity.” There is historical

 8           precedent for regulated firms to recover these costs in rates.

 9                   Two seminal United States Supreme Court cases on the inclusion of cost of capital

10           in what regulated firms charge customers include Bluefield Water Works & Improvement

11           Co. v. Public Service Comm'n 4 and FPC v. Hope Nat. Gas Co. 5. In Bluefield Water Works,

12           the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a utility, in that case a water utility, was allowed to earn

13           a “return on the value of property it employs for the convenience of the public” 6 and that

14           such a return:

15                   …should be reasonably sufficient to assure confidence in the financial
16                   soundness of the utility and should be adequate, under efficient and
17                   economical management, to maintain its credit and enable it to raise the
18                   money necessary for the proper discharge of its public duties. 7

 8        is equal to the discounted value (i.e. accounting for the time value of money) of future

 9        dividends that the shareholder expects to receive over the long term. The discount rate at

10        which those future earnings equal the initial stock price is the cost of equity capital. This

 8   Q.       Please describe the capital asset pricing model.

 9   A        The CAPM model addresses two important concepts: (1) that investments in equity are

10            not “risk-free” investments, therefore equity investors expect a higher return; and (2) that

11            equity investors expect varying return for equity investments of varying risk. The

12            additional return on overall equity market investments, compared to risk-free

13            investments, is what defines the “market risk premium” (or “equity risk premium”). The

14            future premium is unknown but needs to be estimated for this model. The relative risk of

15            different types of equity investments is represented by the company’s “beta,” which is

16            measured by the variance in that company’ stock price relative to the equity market at-

17            large (e.g., the S&P 500). A beta of less than one indicates that investment in that

18            company is relatively less risky than the equity market at large, and that investors in that

19            company should expect a lower return commensurate with lower risk. Conversely, a beta

20            greater than one indicates a riskier venture for which investors should expect a higher

21            return commensurate with that higher risk.
